newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish budget seen more political than prudent.
newsitem.headline: Irish budget seen more political than prudent.

text.p: Irish finance minister Ruairi Quinn's giveaway budget, unveiled on Wednesday, was deemed political rather than economically prudent by economists.
They said Quinn's even-handed tax giveaways were sparked more by concern over a forthcoming election, which must be held before November, than any long term strategy for the economy.
"It is a political budget in terms of the scale of the so-called giveaways and in terms of the distribution across the income spectrum," Davy stockbrokers chief economist Jim O'Leary said.
"It injects a lot of money into an economy that is already booming," Riada economist Dan McLaughlin added. "The risks are all one way."
Quinn introduced the "biggest tax reduction package in the history of the state" in his 1997 annual budget.
He cut the standard tax rate by a percentage point, trimmed pay-related social insurance (PRSI) and widened tax bands.
"The budget will contribute about 2.25 percent to household incomes on an annualised basis and at the margin this will obviously contribute to upward pressure on prices," O'Leary said.
Economists said the expansionary budget was as good as could be expected, given the political cycle and the fact that it was an election year.
McLaughlin believes the budget will effectively boost growth by one percentage point which, although inflation is very low at the moment, it may trigger much higher inflation.

"Ireland has already got significant asset price inflation in the economy. We have house prices up 18 percent year-on-year in the third quarter and the equity market was up 22 percent last year," McLaughlin said. "The risk of a budget like this is that it may exacerbate inflationary pressures."
Economists believe the budget does not do the bond market any favours either.
"The currency is up at a level which few people think can be sustained and is therefore too risky for foreigners to buy the Irish market."
McLaughlin said foreign buying of the Irish bond market was the main force driving that market last year but this was done at much lower levels in the Irish currency against the mark.
"We were below 2.40 marks last year. The problem now is that we are at 2.64 marks and I think it is very difficult for any foreigner to buy the bond market at this level."
Economists said Quinn had the opportunity to do something positive about spending this year if he wanted to take a long term view but he did not.
"He could have used the buoyancy of the economy to run a budget surplus and I think that is what he should have been trying to do because we are not going to keep growing at this rate," O'Leary said.
